title: Breaking the Ice
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article makes the case for using deliberate icebreakers at the start of meeting days, arguing they exist to create comfort for candid discussion rather than merely to entertain. The author dismisses the common objection that icebreakers are hokey or a waste of time, insisting effective ones take 20 minutes or less and simply need to get people talking. It offers a concrete example — the One Word exercise, where participants describe themselves in a single word and then explain their choice — as a fast, low-friction way to prime a group. The piece also notes icebreakers have value in virtual meetings, where initial awkwardness can otherwise linger through an entire session.
points: Icebreakers exist primarily to create comfort for candid discussion, not just to entertain.
Effective icebreakers take 20 minutes or less and require only simple instructions.
The One Word exercise is offered as a concrete, fast example that works for groups of varying sizes.
Meeting days that begin with an icebreaker feel noticeably different from those that skip straight to business.
Even virtual meetings benefit from icebreakers, which reduce the awkwardness common in mediated spaces.
quotes: Getting team members to engage openly and freely right out of the gate is a challenge.
The primary goal of an icebreaker is to make team members more comfortable discussing matters candidly in the very first discussion.
A great icebreaker takes 20 minutes or less and gets people talking to each other.
Once the conversational pump is primed by a good icebreaker, leaders find the group is more comfortable engaging openly throughout the day.
The best icebreakers model energy, comfort, and openness for the rest of the day or meeting.
